To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

antibiotic treatment of humans and mice downregulates expression of RegIIIg (also known as REG3G), a secreted antimicrobial peptide, and that this contributes to susceptibility to infection with vancomycin-resistant enteroccoci (VRE).

broad-spectrum antibiotic treatment decreases intestinal RegIIIγ expression and innate immune defence against VRE, and that Toll-like receptor stimulation restores intestinal RegIIIγ and innate immune defence.
antibiotic-induced downregulation of Reg3γ in the gut mucosa compromises innate immunity and promotes colonization and disease by antibiotic-resistant VRE.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular mechanisms of antibiotic resistance and the development of novel therapies to prevent antibiotic resistance.

the innate immune mechanisms that control the colonization of the intestine by antibiotic-resistant bacteria and how these mechanisms may be exploited to prevent and/or treat infection with antibiotic-resistant pathogens.
the mechanisms by which antibiotics can promote colonization and infection by vancomycin-resistant bacteria, which are a major cause of morbidity and mortality in hospital settings.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
antibiotic treatment of animals down-regulates RegIIIγ expression in the intestinal mucosa.
the use of broad-spectrum antibiotics can cause a down-regulation of RegIII-γ in the intestine, which in turn leads to increased susceptibility of mice towards VRE infection.
antibiotic treatment of the gut compromises mucosal innate immunity and increases the risk of infection by antibiotic-resistant pathogens.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
antibiotic treatment of the host induces a state of immunosuppression that can be exploited by opportunistic pathogens.
antibiotic treatment down-regulates expression of RegIIIgamma in the gut mucosal epithelium.

antibiotic-induced downregulation of Reg3γ, a secreted C-lectin that is critical for innate immune defence against Gram-positive bacteria, is responsible for increased colonization of antibiotic-treated mice by vancomycin-resistant enteroccocci.
The main takeaway from our work is that
antibiotic-induced downregulation of the innate immune defence protein RegIIIγ promotes VRE colonization and infection.
antibiotic treatment of patients can increase their risk for infection with antibiotic-resistant bacteria by downregulating the expression of RegIIIg.

the use of broad spectrum antibiotics, such as vancoycin, can compromise innate immune defenses, which can lead to increased susceptibility to infection by antibiotic resistant microbes, such as vanomycin-resistant Enterococci.
